title: Food Chain, Food Web and Ecological Pyramids
topicTitle: Food chain, food web, trophic level, ecological pyramids, productivity
notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — How Energy Moves Through Life

Every ecosystem runs on one currency: energy, entering as sunlight and leaving as heat, passing from plants to herbivores to carnivores. Food chains and webs trace that flow; pyramids depict it; productivity measures it. This topic carries more NEB questions than any other in ecology — including a numerical.

## 2. Food Chain, Food Web and Trophic Levels

### 2.1 Food chain — the linear energy path

**Grazing food chain (starts with living plants):**
Grass → Grasshopper → Frog → Snake → Hawk
(Producer → Primary consumer → Secondary → Tertiary → Top carnivore)

**Detritus food chain (starts with dead matter):**
Dead leaves → Detritivores (earthworm, woodlice) → Decomposer bacteria/fungi → Small carnivores → Top carnivore

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Trophic level** | Position in the chain (T1 producers, T2 herbivores, T3 carnivores…) |
| **Standing crop** | Total biomass at a trophic level at a time |
| **10% law (Lindeman, 1942)** | Only ~10% of energy transfers to the next level; the rest is lost as heat, respiration, excretion |

**Why chains are short:** with only ~10% passing on, after 4–5 transfers too little energy remains to support another level — hence top carnivores are rare.

### 2.2 Food web vs food chain (NEB 2024)

| Basis | Food chain | Food web |
|---|---|---|
| Definition | Single linear sequence of who-eats-whom | Interconnected network of many food chains |
| Structure | One pathway of energy | Many interlocking pathways |
| Stability | Fragile — remove one link and the chain breaks | Stable — alternative pathways buffer loss |
| Realism | Theoretical simplification | What nature actually contains |
| Example | Grass → grasshopper → frog → snake → hawk | Grassland web: grass eaten by insects, rabbits, cattle; each preyed on by several predators |

### 2.3 The ten percent law applied

If producers fix 10,000 kJ: herbivores get ~1,000 kJ, small carnivores ~100 kJ, top carnivores ~10 kJ. This explains (1) short chains, (2) small top-predator populations, (3) large human grain consumption being more efficient than meat-heavy diets.

## 3. Ecological Pyramids (NEB 2024 + 2023)

**Definition:** graphical representation of a trophic parameter (number, biomass, energy) with producers at the base and top carnivores at the apex.

| Pyramid | Base → apex | Usually upright? | Can invert? |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Pyramid of numbers** | Count of individuals | Usually | **Yes** — one big tree supports thousands of insects (parasitic food chain); a banyan → herbivores → parasites inverts it |
| **Pyramid of biomass** | Dry weight (g/m²) | Usually in terrestrial systems | **Yes** in aquatic systems — a small standing crop of phytoplankton supports a larger zooplankton mass at a moment in time (fast turnover) |
| **Pyramid of energy** | Energy (kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹) | **Always upright — never inverted** | Never |

**Why the energy pyramid is always upright (NEB 2024):** energy flows one way — at each transfer ~90% is lost as heat (respiration, excretion, egestion), and heat cannot be recycled back. So each successive level must hold less energy than the one below; a higher level can never contain more energy than its food source. Numbers and biomass are snapshots (invertible); energy is a rate measured over time (never invertible).

## 4. Productivity

| Term | Definition | Unit |
|---|---|---|
| **GPP (Gross Primary Productivity)** | Total solar energy fixed by producers | kcal m⁻² yr⁻¹ |
| **NPP (Net Primary Productivity)** | GPP − plant respiration (R); the energy actually stored, available to consumers | kcal m⁻² yr⁻¹ |
| **Secondary productivity** | Energy stored by consumers | kcal m⁻² yr⁻¹ |

**NPP = GPP − R** — the most-tested formula in ecology.

### 4.1 Worked example (NEB 2022)

Grassland: GPP = 4800 kcal m⁻² yr⁻¹; plant respiration = 1200 kcal m⁻² yr⁻¹.
**NPP = 4800 − 1200 = 3600 kcal m⁻² yr⁻¹.**
If herbivores consume 20% of NPP: energy reaching herbivores = 0.20 × 3600 = **720 kcal m⁻² yr⁻¹**.

### 4.2 Productivity by ecosystem

| Ecosystem | NPP | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Tropical rainforest | Highest terrestrial (~2000+ g/m²/yr) | Warm + wet all year |
| Coral reefs, estuaries | Very high aquatic | Nutrient-rich shallow water |
| Open ocean | Low per m², but huge total area | Nutrient-limited |
| Deserts | Very low | Water-limited |

**Food chain vs web; GPP vs NPP — the paired concepts**

| Concept pair | First term | Second term | Exam distinction |
|---|---|---|---|
| Chain vs web | Food chain: one linear feeding sequence | Food web: interconnected chains | Webs show real ecosystems; chains are teaching models |
| GPP vs NPP | GPP: total energy fixed by photosynthesis | NPP = GPP − respiration (R) | Only NPP is available to consumers |
| Trophic level | Position in feeding sequence (T1, T2...) | Each level loses ~90% of energy | Caps chains at 4-5 levels |
| Pyramid types | Number, biomass, energy | Energy is always upright | Inverted examples: tree ecosystem (numbers), sea (biomass) |

## 5. Conceptual Relationships

- **Topic 21 → here:** interactions assemble into feeding links.
- **Here → Topic 23:** pond and forest ecosystems are worked examples of these flows.
- **Here → biogeochemical cycles (Topic 24):** energy flows one way and is lost; **matter cycles** — the great asymmetry of ecosystems.
- **Here → Topic 26:** disrupting pyramids (overfishing top carnivores) and adding nutrients (eutrophication) are human imbalances.

## 6. Exam Orientation and Previous Year Questions (NEB)

### 6.1 Verified PYQs from the solved-paper bank

| Year | Unit | Topic | Question | Marks | Type |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2080/2024 | Ecology | Food chain/web | Distinguish between a food chain and a food web. What is the ten percent law? | 3 | Difference + definition |
| 2080/2024 | Ecology | Pyramids | What are ecological pyramids? Explain why the pyramid of energy is always upright. | 3 | Short answer |
| 2079/2023 | Ecology | Pyramids | Differentiate between the pyramid of numbers and the pyramid of biomass, and state one case in which each becomes inverted. | 2 | Difference |
| 2078/2022 | Ecology | Productivity | Grassland GPP 4800, respiration 1200 — calculate NPP (and follow-ups). | 3 | Numerical |

### 6.2 Model answers

**Q1 (3m) — Food chain vs food web + ten percent law.**
Answer: A **food chain** is a single linear sequence of energy transfer (grass → grasshopper → frog → snake → hawk), while a **food web** is the interconnected network of many food chains in an ecosystem, giving alternative pathways and stability. The **ten percent law (Lindeman)** states that only about 10% of the energy at one trophic level is transferred to the next; ~90% is lost as heat through respiration, excretion and egestion — which is why chains rarely exceed 4–5 levels.

**Q2 (3m) — Ecological pyramids; why energy pyramid is always upright.**
Answer: Ecological pyramids graph trophic parameters — numbers, biomass or energy — with producers at the base. The **pyramid of energy is always upright** because energy flows unidirectionally: at each transfer about 90% is dissipated as heat, and heat cannot be recycled, so each higher level necessarily contains less energy than the one below it. Numbers and biomass are momentary snapshots and can invert (one tree → many insects; phytoplankton → zooplankton), but energy is a rate over time and can never increase upward.

**Q3 (2m) — Pyramid of numbers vs biomass + inversion cases.**
Answer: The **pyramid of numbers** counts individuals per level (usually upright; inverted when one large tree supports many herbivorous insects and their parasites). The **pyramid of biomass** uses dry weight per level (usually upright on land; inverted in open ocean where a small standing crop of phytoplankton supports a larger zooplankton biomass because phytoplankton reproduce rapidly).

**Q4 (3m) — NPP numerical.**
Answer: NPP = GPP − R = 4800 − 1200 = **3600 kcal m⁻² yr⁻¹**. (If asked: energy to herbivores at 20% consumption = 720 kcal m⁻² yr⁻¹; at 10% transfer, secondary consumers receive ~72 kcal m⁻² yr⁻¹.)

### 6.3 Common examination mistakes

1. Inverting the energy pyramid "like biomass" — never; give the one-way heat-loss reason.
2. Writing NPP = GPP + R — it is **minus**.
3. Confusing trophic level numbering (producers are T1, not T0).
4. Forgetting units (kcal m⁻² yr⁻¹) in numericals — units carry marks.
5. Describing the food web as "a long food chain" — it is a network, not a chain.

**Standing crop vs productivity:** standing crop = biomass at an instant (snapshot); productivity = rate of production over time (movie).
**Grazing vs detritus chain:** grazing starts with living plants; detritus starts with dead organic matter — in forests the detritus chain dominates.
practice:
Why is a meat-heavy human diet ecologically expensive?

**Answer.** By the **10% law**, only about one-tenth of the energy at each trophic level reaches the next. Eating grain directly puts a person at T2 and harvests ~10× more energy per hectare than eating grain-fed animals, which puts the person at T3. A meat-heavy diet therefore demands far more land, water and primary production to deliver the same calories — it supports fewer people per hectare and leaves a larger ecological footprint.

mcqs.question: The ten percent law was proposed by:
mcqs.explanation: Lindeman (1942) quantified trophic energy transfer at roughly 10% per level.

mcqs.question: Which pyramid can never be inverted?
mcqs.explanation: Energy is a one-way flow measured as a rate — each level must have less than the one below.

mcqs.question: A food web is more stable than a food chain because:
mcqs.explanation: If one prey declines, predators switch — the network redistributes pressure.

mcqs.question: GPP is 6000 and respiration 2500 kcal m⁻²yr⁻¹. NPP is:
The inverted pyramid of numbers is seen in:
mcqs.explanation: A single large tree supports many herbivorous insects and their parasites — apex counts exceed base.

mcqs.question: In the chain grass→deer→tiger, the tiger is at trophic level:
mcqs.explanation: Grass T1, deer T2 (herbivore), tiger T3 (secondary/terminal carnivore).

mcqs.question: Detritus food chains begin with:
mcqs.explanation: Detritivores and decomposers process dead matter — the dominant chain in forests.

mcqs.question: If producers fix 10,000 kJ, the energy reaching herbivores is about:
mcqs.explanation: Ten percent law: only ~10% passes each level — 10,000 (T1) → 1,000 kJ (T2 herbivores).

notes: Food chain: a linear sequence of organisms where each is eaten by the next; transfers energy and matter (sun → producer → primary consumer → secondary consumer → tertiary consumer).
Food web: a network of interconnected food chains; more realistic than a single chain; shows multiple feeding relationships.
Trophic levels: TL1 producers (autotrophs), TL2 primary consumers (herbivores), TL3 secondary consumers (carnivores), TL4+ tertiary consumers.
Ecological pyramids: number (pyramid of numbers), biomass (pyramid of biomass), energy (pyramid of energy).
Pyramid of energy: always upright; each level has less energy than the one below (10% rule).
Pyramid of numbers: usually upright; can be inverted (e.g., one tree supports many insects).
Pyramid of biomass: usually upright; can be inverted in aquatic ecosystems (phytoplankton turn over fast).
Productivity: gross primary productivity (GPP = total photosynthesis), net primary productivity (NPP = GPP − plant respiration).
Consumer productivity: energy assimilated by consumers per unit time.
NEB focus: food chain, food web, trophic levels, ecological pyramids, and productivity.
confusion: A food chain is LINEAR; a food web is a NETWORK of chains (more realistic).
Producers (plants, phytoplankton) are at trophic level 1; herbivores at level 2; carnivores at level 3+.
The pyramid of ENERGY is always upright; the pyramids of numbers and biomass CAN be inverted.
An inverted pyramid of numbers occurs when one large organism supports many small ones (e.g., a tree with many insects).
An inverted pyramid of biomass occurs in aquatic ecosystems where phytoplankton (producers) have low standing biomass but high turnover.
The 10% rule: only ~10% of energy transfers from one trophic level to the next; ~90% is lost as heat.

universalFacts: The 10% rule (Lindeman, 1942) explains why food chains are usually 4–5 trophic levels long.
A pyramid of energy is ALWAYS upright because energy is lost at each transfer (heat, respiration).
Phytoplankton in the ocean produce ~50% of Earth's oxygen (GPP of aquatic ecosystems).
NPP is the energy available to consumers (herbivores) in an ecosystem.
examples: Grassland food chain: grass → rabbit → fox → eagle (4 trophic levels).
Pond food web: algae → mosquito larva → frog → snake → eagle; also algae → zooplankton → small fish → big fish.
Inverted pyramid of numbers: one oak tree (TL1) → many aphids (TL2) → a few ladybirds (TL3).
Inverted pyramid of biomass: phytoplankton (TL1) → zooplankton (TL2) → small fish (TL3) in the ocean.
Productivity: GPP = 1000 gC/m²/yr; plant respiration = 500 gC/m²/yr → NPP = 500 gC/m²/yr.

originalContent.summary: Energy and matter flow through ecosystems in food chains (linear) and food webs (networks). Trophic levels (producers → primary consumers → secondary → tertiary) structure these. Ecological pyramids (number, biomass, energy) visualise trophic structure; the pyramid of energy is always upright because ~90% of energy is lost at each transfer (10% rule). Productivity (GPP, NPP) measures the rate of energy capture and availability to consumers. NEB focuses on food chains, food webs, trophic levels, the three pyramids, and productivity calculations.
